newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban warn journalists over reports.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban warn journalists over reports.

text.p: The purist Islamic Taleban movement, rulers of most of Afghanistan for the last two weeks, accused foreign journalists of distorting news about them and issued a veiled warning of reprisals if such reports continued.

Apparently rattled by its first military setbacks since the movement took Kabul and nearby cities in a lightning campaign last month, the movement's information minister warned foreign journalists against carrying reports he called "baseless".

"I would like to comment on news which has been broadcast over the last two days...and I would like to point out that you should refrain from broadcasting these kinds of news," Amir Khan Mutaqi told a news conference.

The Taleban, which is still in the process of appointing its followers to key government positions, has been unsure how to handle an influx of foreign journalists to cover the latest twist in Afghanistan's long-running civil war.

Although most journalists have been allowed into the country, many have been barred from travelling to the front line since the movement's military momentum against ousted government forces in the north slowed earlier this week.

Mutaqi, who said he had visited the front line earlier on Thursday, dismissed news reports that the Taleban had suffered reverses in its battles against ousted military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, whose forces hold the strategic Panjsher valley.
Travellers and aid workers said Masood's forces had inflicted heavy casualties on the Taleban in the past two days.

"The news that was broadcast by international media that heavy losses were inflicted on the Taleban and many of the Taleban died was completely baseless and whoever has broadcast these news has committed a moral crime," Mutaqi said,
"Therefore I advise you not to release any news that has not been confirmed by the concerned authorities of the Taleban."

The bearded Mutaqi is the main spokesman for the secretive Taleban administration, whose purist brand of Islam forbids most women to work, most girls to study and requires men to pray five times a day.

Refusing to allow cameras to film his news conferences, he has launched almost daily broadsides against western countries for being slow to recognise his government and against foreign agencies for distorting his government's Islamic policies.
But Thursday's attack on the media, which singled out the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) and Voice of America, appeared to be the harshest assault yet on foreign journalists.
"You are always in the search of details and ignore the positive developments which the government makes," he said.

"I am astonished why the international media attach no importance to the achievements of the Taleban, for instance when they took Sarobi and advanced on Kabul there was not enough publicity, whereas when our enemies make a very minor gain it is given wide publicity."

He reminded journalists of the expulsion from the town of Herat last year of a BBC journalist after reports that upset the local Taleban leaders. But he denied that his reminder of that incident constituted a threat.
"We highly respect the journalists and this is a request and it is the responsibility of journalists not to release false news," he said,
